  re-running `parts=all` a third time and re-paying for bands that already passed.
- **The OCR guard's `MIN_CONFIDENCE` was RAISED 55 -> 85 by Dev on 2026-08-14**,
  after every hit across all nine concepts turned out to be a false positive in
  a 55-83 band while real composited labels scored 91-96. There has never been
  a true positive above 83. The cost of 55 was real: d06's room never passed
  once in nine attempts, and d09 lost a whole concept — two already-paid,
  already-passing bands discarded — to ('wake', 60.0) on a linen weave.
  The standing rule that the model must never render type is UNCHANGED: the
  prompt still excludes text, the guard still runs on every image, and genuine
  legible words score far above 85. **Still to confirm on the next Actions run:
  the both-directions validation (a labelled card must still FAIL) has not been
  re-run at 85 — pytesseract is not installed locally.** If a real rendered word
  ever slips through below 85, lower it again and record the sample.
- Room exposure varies with each concept's own palette reflectance under an
  identical lighting prompt — 84.5 (d01) vs 111.6 (d02) mean luminance. Only
  matters if consistent mood across the series becomes a requirement.
- Swatch-to-room material drift, the most persistent issue in the series, now has
  a working method. **Compare HUE AND SATURATION SEPARATELY — raw RGB distance is
  the wrong metric** and is what made this look unfixable for six concepts. Since
  ROOM_LIGHT v6 the room is deliberately lamplit while `BAND_LIGHT` keeps the
  bands flat and evenly lit for label legibility, so every material measures
  darker in the room than on its tile, and raw RGB distance mostly reports that
  lighting difference rather than any real mismatch. On d07 raw distance said all
  three bands drifted (63 / 27 / 37); split apart, hue was already correct on all
  three and only saturation was off.
  Worked example, d07 retuned via `parts=bands` against the approved room:
  walnut went from S=95 (fiery orange-red) against the room's 63, to within 17;
  travertine from S=1 (dead neutral grey) against the room's 20, to within 12;
  hue within 1-5 degrees on all three. The travertine was also renamed from
  "Silver Travertine" to "Roman Travertine" because the approved room shows warm
  cream stone, not silver — **check the band NAME against the room too, not just
  its colour.**
  A tile will never match a moody room on BRIGHTNESS and should not be made to;
  `BAND_LIGHT` stays flat. Hue and saturation are the things that can match.
  Historical raw-distance figures, kept for context but not comparable to the
  above: d02 walnut 71 and travertine 79, d03 alabaster 77, d02 limewash 14.
- Room shots contain gibberish lettering on book spines that OCR passes as clean.
  Flagged, undecided.
- **The d-series room prompt is ~533 words, well past BFL's own recommended
  ceiling** (their "long" band tops out around 300, with an explicit warning that
  more words do not mean better results). Untouched because five concepts were
  approved at roughly this length, but it is a plausible contributor to styling
  drift and to instructions being only partly obeyed. Raise with Dev before
  adding anything further to that prompt.
- **d06's room shot was re-rolled rather than edited further, at Dev's call.** The
  edited version fixed the console-through-bench intersection but only partly
  complied on the urns (off the walkway, still on the treads) and restyled them
  in the process. The re-roll under `SPATIAL_RULE` came back clean on all three
  samples and is what is committed. The edited version is not lost — it is in
  git history at `a494b11`, recoverable with
  `git checkout a494b11 -- concept_review/d06/d06_foyer_cobalt_app.png`.
- **d06 has now tripped the OCR no-text guard 9 times out of 9 room-shot
  attempts**, across three separate runs (two `parts=all`, one `parts=room`),
  every hit low-confidence garbage on zellige tile and stair ironwork. Its room
  shot has never once passed the guard, and every committed version of it has
  been placed by hand after visual inspection. This is the strongest single piece
  of evidence yet that `MIN_CONFIDENCE` is miscalibrated for ornate pattern.
  Still not changed unilaterally — but d06 is the concept to point at when
  deciding.

## Single Product Reel — the third content type (2026-08-14)

Added `single_product_reel/single_product_pipeline.py` and
`.github/workflows/single-product-reel.yml` for a format neither the original
swatch+application rotation (`core_decor_reel_pipeline.py`) nor Hot Takes
(`hot_takes/`) cover: a ONE-OFF product drop from a Drive folder Dev points it
at, containing exactly one swatch photo and any number of application photos
of that same product — not the committed `assets/` pool, not a paired
swatch/application filename convention.

Built the same way Hot Takes was built alongside the original pipeline: reuses
every shared stage (Drive fetching, audio mastering, template cut-timing
extraction, Meta/Buffer publishing, repo hosting, the git-backed counter
helper) directly from `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py`, with its own
`single_product_reel/template_index.txt` so its position in the Drive Template
Reels rotation never collides with the other two pipelines' counters — same
reasoning already recorded above for Hot Takes' own `_fetch_template_for_audio`.

**Reel structure**: segment 0 is always the swatch (the anticipation beat),
every later segment is `random.choice(application_photos)` chosen WITH
replacement — repeats across segments are expected and correct, not a bug, per
Dev's literal instruction ("cycle through all the applications randomly even
they repeat"). Because the swatch only ever appears in segment 0, the reel is
guaranteed to end on an application shot for any template with 2+ cuts, with
none of `core.build_reel`'s parity/alternation bookkeeping needed — that
bookkeeping exists there specifically to keep a fixed swatch/application PAIR
alternating correctly, which doesn't apply here.

**Swatch detection**: whichever file in the folder has `"swatch"` in its name
(case-insensitive). If none match, falls back to the first file alphabetically
and logs a warning — worth checking on the first run of a new folder that
doesn't follow this naming convention, since a silent wrong guess here would
mean an application photo gets used as the opening "material" shot instead of
the actual swatch.

**Product name**: `PRODUCT_NAME` workflow input if given, otherwise the Drive
folder's own display name via the new `drive_upload.get_folder_name()`. Rename
the Drive folder to something caption-worthy before dispatching if the raw
folder name wouldn't read well in a caption.

**"A song already in our library"**: resolved with Dev as meaning the next
Template Reel in the existing Drive Template Reels rotation — its mastered
audio AND its real cut-timing, exactly the mechanism the other two pipelines
already use. There is no separate music library in this repo; every track this
project has ever posted with came from that same folder.

**Captions, per Dev's instruction, deliberately two different shapes** — see
the new functions in `caption_bank.py`:
  - `get_link_in_bio_caption(product_name)` → Instagram, Facebook, TikTok,
    YouTube. Short hook + a natural link-in-bio CTA naming the product, same
    "don't read as AI-written" voice as `get_caption()` but no rotation index
    (this is a one-off run, not a pool to cycle through without repeats).
  - `get_pinterest_seo_caption(product_name)` → Pinterest only. Deliberately
    long and keyword-front-loaded, not just a longer version of the other
    caption — Pinterest's own search surfaces reward descriptive, keyword-dense
    pin text, and front-load the product name + keywords since Pinterest
    truncates descriptions in search results.

**Pinterest publishes via Buffer** (`core.publish_to_buffer(..., platform=
"pinterest")`) — Dev confirmed Pinterest is already a connected Buffer channel,
referenced as the new `BUFFER_PINTEREST_CHANNEL_ID` secret, same as the
existing `BUFFER_TIKTOK_CHANNEL_ID` / `BUFFER_YOUTUBE_CHANNEL_ID` pattern.
Deliberately uses `publish_to_buffer`'s plain minimal path — caption text + one
video asset, no extra `metadata` block — rather than guessing at a
title/board field the way the YouTube branch does for `categoryId`/`privacy`.
Buffer's exact GraphQL input schema for Pinterest posts (title separate from
description? board selection, or does the channel already imply one board?)
has never been tested against this project's real Buffer account. Dev's own
words: "it's okay if you can't write a custom caption for it, I can probably
update it later" — so the first real run through this workflow IS the test;
if Buffer rejects or mishandles the Pinterest post, add the missing metadata
field to the `if platform == "pinterest":` branch of `publish_to_buffer()`
afterward, the same way the YouTube branch was built, rather than guessing now.

This workflow is `workflow_dispatch` only, no schedule — same "deliberate act"
reasoning as `generate-concept.yml`: it corresponds to one specific Drive
folder Dev has just pointed it at, not a recurring rotation.

## Carousel Post — the fourth content type (2026-08-17, multi-concept 2026-08-18)

Added `carousel_post/carousel_pipeline.py`, `carousel_post/prepare_image.py`
and `.github/workflows/carousel-post.yml` for a format none of the first
three content types cover: a static multi-IMAGE carousel, not a video. Each
post cycles through `CONCEPTS_PER_CAROUSEL` (4) c-series concepts, and each
concept contributes its own swatch-then-application pair in order — the
same "swatch is the anticipation beat, application is the payoff" reveal
logic already used throughout the video reel pipelines, repeated per concept
across the carousel instead of a single pair. No audio, no cut-timing, no
ffmpeg, no librosa at all. First content type in the repo that needs none of
them.

**Originally shipped as ONE concept per post (2 images).** Dev's instruction
2026-08-18: a carousel should be multiple slides showing more than one
concept, not just one swatch+application pair. `run_pipeline()` now reads
`CONCEPT_INDEX_FILE` as a START index, takes `CONCEPTS_PER_CAROUSEL`
consecutive concepts (wrapping via modulo, same as before), and advances the
counter by however many concepts were actually used — not by 1 — so the
rotation still covers every concept exactly once per full cycle regardless of
batch size. 4 concepts = 8 images per post, safely under Instagram's 10-child
carousel limit. `publish_carousel_to_instagram` already took an arbitrary-
length `image_urls` list (no code change needed there beyond a docstring
update) — the 2-image assumption only lived in the caller.

**Scope is deliberately the ORIGINAL c-series only (c01-c50)**, filtered out
of the same `assets/swatches` / `assets/application` folders the d-series now
also lives in — `carousel_pipeline._c_series_pairs()` reuses
`core._pair_swatches_with_applications()` then keeps only stems starting with
`"c"`. Dev asked for this against the c-series specifically; nothing stops a
d-series carousel from being a later, separate decision the way d-series
video publishing will be.

**Own counters**, both under `carousel_post/`: `concept_index.txt` and
`caption_index.txt`. Same reasoning already recorded above for Hot Takes —
reusing the root-level `concept_offset.txt`/`caption_index.txt` would race
this pipeline's position against the main daily pipeline's whenever both run
close together. `caption_index.txt` here is a plain unbounded increment (no
modulo applied before writing), matching how the main pipeline's own
`advance_caption_index` behaves — `caption_bank.get_caption()` already mods
everything it needs internally.

### The JPEG + aspect-ratio problem — READ THIS, the approach changed once already

This project's swatch/application assets are 1072x1920 (9:16, ratio 0.5625) —
built for the video reels. Two real constraints, confirmed against Meta's own
current docs before writing any code (not assumed): the content-publishing
API accepts **JPEG only** — a PNG `image_url` is rejected outright — and feed/
carousel images must fall within a **4:5 to 1.91:1** aspect ratio. 9:16 is far
outside that band on both counts.

**v1 — fit-inside + blurred pillarbox — shipped, posted for real, then
rejected on the actual live result.** Since 4:5 (0.8) is proportionally WIDER
per unit height than 9:16 (0.5625), the reasoning was: fit the WHOLE source
inside a 4:5 canvas by shrinking to the HEIGHT, and fill the empty left/right
space with a blurred, darkened extension of the same image (the technique
Instagram's own app uses when a taller photo is posted to feed) — content-
preserving by construction, nothing ever cropped. It worked exactly as
designed and still looked wrong: Dev's verdict on the first real post was
that the blurred side bars just read as empty space, not a considered design
choice. **Content preservation was optimized for at the expense of the actual
visual result — worth remembering before re-deriving "never crop, only pad"
as obviously correct on the next image-shape problem.**

**v2 — current — full-bleed COVER crop, anchored to protect the swatch
label.** Dev's instruction after seeing v1 live: losing some top/bottom is
fine, as long as the swatch card's material-name text stays visible. Scale
the source to COVER the 4:5 canvas completely (width is always the binding
dimension for this project's 9:16-into-4:5 case, so overflow is always in
HEIGHT) and crop the overflow — `prepare_carousel_image(src, dest, anchor_y)`
in `prepare_image.py`, where `anchor_y` places the crop window vertically
(0.0 keeps the top, 1.0 keeps the bottom, 0.5 is centered). `carousel_
pipeline.py` calls it with **anchor_y=1.0 for the swatch** — crop only ever
comes off the TOP, so the label (bottom fifth of frame on c01) survives
regardless of exactly where it sits on any given concept — and **anchor_y=0.5
for the application shot**, a normal centered crop, since it has no
text-survival constraint. Verified by eye against c01's real assets after the
change: full-bleed on both images, no side bars, and the swatch label sits
comfortably inside the frame with margin to spare.

### Publishing shape is genuinely different per platform, not just "post the image"

Added to `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py` rather than inside `carousel_post/`,
since these lean on the exact same `_graph_post`/`_graph_get`/`PipelineError`
plumbing already centralized there — genuinely shared, not content-type-
specific, same bar as everything else that lives in that file rather than a
subfolder.

- **Instagram** (`publish_carousel_to_instagram`) — a different container
  SHAPE from the REELS path, not a variant of it: each image becomes its own
  `is_carousel_item` child container first, then one parent container with
  `media_type=CAROUSEL` and `children` referencing all child ids gets
  published. Order is preserved exactly as passed in.
- **Facebook** (`publish_photo_post_to_facebook`) — Facebook Pages have no
  carousel object at all. The equivalent is an ordinary `/feed` post with
  multiple photos attached: upload each photo UNPUBLISHED first
  (`published=false` to `/{page_id}/photos`) so it doesn't appear as its own
  standalone post, then one `/feed` post with `attached_media` referencing all
  the resulting photo ids. Facebook's own UI renders this as a swipeable
  gallery.
- **TikTok / Pinterest** (`publish_image_carousel_to_buffer`) — best-effort,
  attempted via Buffer, same as everything else this project reaches through
  Buffer rather than a direct API. **UNVERIFIED against this project's real
  Buffer account as of when this was written** — same "first real run is the
  test" position already taken for the Pinterest video path in
  `single_product_reel` (see that section above). The asset shape
  (`{"image": {"url": ...}}` per entry, ordered list for multiple images) is
  confirmed from Buffer's own current API docs, not guessed — what's NOT
  confirmed is whether Buffer actually surfaces multiple image assets as a
  real swipeable carousel on TikTok's "photo mode" or a Pinterest multi-image
  pin for THIS project's connected channels, versus posting only the first
  image, or rejecting multi-image assets outright for a given channel type.
  **A failure here does not fail the run** — `carousel_pipeline.run_pipeline()`
  wraps both calls in try/except and only logs a warning, since IG and FB are
  the proven, required platforms for this format and shouldn't be blocked by
  an unverified extra path. If either misbehaves on a real run, check the
  actual response body before assuming the schema is wrong.
- **YouTube — not attempted at all**, unlike TikTok/Pinterest. This project's
  YouTube channel is wired via Buffer for Shorts VIDEO content only, and there
  is no image/carousel post surface available through that same channel. This
  isn't "untested", it's "not a thing this integration can do" — don't add a
  speculative attempt here the way TikTok/Pinterest have one.

### Schedule

`.github/workflows/carousel-post.yml`, Tuesday and Friday at 16:00 UTC — twice
a week per Dev's request. Placeholder day/time, same status as every other
schedule in this repo (14:00 UTC daily-reel, 18:00 UTC every-2-days
hot-takes) — deliberately offset from both so nothing lands in the same
window, revisit once there's engagement data.

**Confirmed working end-to-end, first real post this pipeline ever made.**
Manually dispatched via `workflow_dispatch` right after the multi-concept
change above shipped, specifically to verify it against real accounts, not
just compiled code. 4 concepts (c02_kit_scandi, c03_kit_indloft,
c04_kit_mtnlux, c05_kit_brut), 8 images, one carousel:

- **Instagram**: media_id `18127461283686439` — succeeded.
- **Facebook**: post_id `..._122122971933091378` — succeeded.
- **TikTok via Buffer**: post_id `6a846040033c29724fd00e12` — succeeded.
  First real confirmation that `publish_image_carousel_to_buffer`'s
  multi-image asset shape actually works for TikTok photo-mode on this
  project's connected channel; it was previously speculative (see above).
- **Pinterest**: skipped — `BUFFER_PINTEREST_CHANNEL_ID` isn't set in this

  `concept_index.txt` 1 → 5, `caption_index.txt` 1 → 2.

configured). Caption content is identical across every platform attempted,

platform-native.

## Caption bank and Hot Takes opinion pool expanded (2026-08-18)

Dev asked for more non-boring variation in both pools — repetition was
becoming noticeable across runs.

- `caption_bank.py`: `HOOKS` 30 → 48, `TAILS` 20 → 30. `cycle_length()`
  (`len(HOOKS) * len(TAILS)`) went from 600 to 1440 before hook/tail
  combinations repeat. New entries follow the same v2 voice rules the module
  docstring already lays out — varied rhythm, no forced hook+CTA+hashtag-wall
  template, occasional lowercase starts, real-person asides rather than
  directive CTAs. No code change needed; `get_caption()` already derives its
  modulo math from `len(HOOKS)`/`len(TAILS)` directly.
- `hot_takes/opinion_bank.py`: `OPINIONS` 25 → 44. The original 25 were all
  the same "They: dismissive line / Me: pushback" shape; the new entries keep
  every pair a two-line setup/punchline (that's load-bearing — see
  `render_text_block`'s 1.6s reveal gap) but vary the joke structure itself
  (not every line opens with "They:"), while still passing the file's
  DELIBERATELY GENERIC test — no color/material references, so any entry
  still reads correctly over any of the 50 application photos.

## Dolly Reel — the fifth content type (2026-08-18), LIVE IN THE SCHEDULE

Dev shared a real reference clip and asked to test a new reel concept: a
continuous forward dolly push-in through a room, named with real VFX terms —
"2.5D Parallax Zoom", "3D Camera Projection Push/Pull", "Vertigo Effect" —
built from application photos only (no swatches), stitched clips forming one
reel, more than one concept per reel.

### What the reference clip actually showed, checked by pulling real frames

Downloaded via the user's uploads path, analyzed with `ffprobe`/`ffmpeg`
frame extraction (not eyeballed at native playback speed) since no video-
watching tool is available. 720x1280, 30fps, 16.1s. The last ~5.5s was an
"instasave"-style repost bumper (Instagram icon reveal + `@IY_ARCH` handle)
tacked on by whatever tool downloaded it — not part of the actual shot.
The real creative content, 0–10s, is a single continuous **forward dolly
push** — no pan, no pull-back, despite those being named in the brief.
Worth knowing if this ever gets re-analyzed: the brief's "push-in then
pull-back + pan" doesn't describe THIS reference clip; it's a one-way push
the whole way through.

### The real technical question: can real parallax come from a single static AI photo?

Yes, in principle — this is genuinely established technique (Meta's old "3D
Photos" feature, LeiaPix, the published "3D Ken Burns Effect" research all do
exactly this from one still image, AI-generated or real; it only needs a
depth map, doesn't care about the photo's origin). Two prototypes were built
and tested locally against a real application photo (`c01_kit_modlux_app.png`)
to find out whether it was ACHIEVABLE HERE, not just possible in theory —
throwaway scripts, kept at `concept_tools/_test_parallax.py` and
`concept_tools/_test_layered_parallax.py` as documented evidence, not wired
into any pipeline:

- **Depth estimation itself works well.** `depth-anything/Depth-Anything-V2-Small-hf`
  via `transformers`, CPU-only, ~2s/image after the model is cached (~7s
  cold). The depth map came out accurate on the first try — foreground
  counter/stools/floor read near, the far wall/window read far, verified by
  eye against the depth visualization, not assumed.
- **Test B — continuous per-pixel depth-weighted zoom** (an inverse-warp
  trick: each pixel's own local zoom scales with its own depth value).
  Produced real parallax separation but visibly BENT every straight line by
  the final frame — window mullions, countertop edges, cabinet fronts all
  curved. Not acceptable against this brand's architectural photography.
- **Test C — layered parallax** (3 discrete depth bands — background/
  midground/foreground — each a RIGID center-zoom of the same full photo,
  blended with depth-driven soft weights; the classic multiplane-camera
  trick). Fixed the bent-lines problem — straight lines stay straight within
  a layer by construction — but produced visible dark ghosting/double-edge
  halos at every depth boundary (the pendant lights, the chair, the
  counter-to-window edge): two differently-scaled copies of the same photo
  not quite lining up where layers blend.
- **Root cause, same in both**: genuine depth-based parallax needs true 3D
  reprojection (rendering from a moving virtual camera against the depth map
  as a surface) PLUS inpainting the small slivers of background revealed
  from behind foreground objects as the camera pushes in — real information
  that doesn't exist in a single 2D photo and has to be synthesized. Neither
  test did that; both are 2D approximations, which is exactly why both show
  artifacts. A proper implementation is real additional engineering (a
  dedicated inpainting model or a lighter OpenCV fill, neither built or
  tested here) with an unproven payoff.

**Dev's call after seeing the side-by-side**: drop true parallax, ship the
plain Ken Burns push-in (test A — zero geometric artifacts, matches the
"push-in" half of the brief exactly, costs nothing extra to run). True
parallax stays possible as a future investment if ever revisited — the two
test scripts above are the starting point, not proof it can't be done, just
proof the cheap version isn't clean enough for this brand's photography.

### What was actually built

`dolly_reel/dolly_reel_pipeline.py` — structurally Hot Takes' beat-synced-
montage shape (reuses the Drive Template Reels rotation for audio AND real
cut-timing via `core.extract_template_cut_timestamps`, one application photo
per detected cut segment), not the original swatch+application pipeline's
shape. `compute_segment_boundaries` is a deliberate copy of
`hot_takes_pipeline`'s function of the same name, not an import — sibling
content-type modules in this repo only import `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py`,
never each other. Own counters, all under `dolly_reel/`: `application_index.txt`,
`template_index.txt`, `caption_index.txt` — same collision-avoidance reasoning
already recorded above for Hot Takes and Carousel Post.

**The one genuinely new piece**: `_pushin_clip()` — plain ffmpeg `zoompan`,
supersampled 3x before the zoom (so the crop window doesn't visibly soften at
the most-zoomed-in frame), zoom RATE fixed per second
(`ZOOM_RATE_PER_SECOND = 0.07`, matching the tested feel of 1.0→1.35 over 5s)
rather than a fixed end-zoom, so segments of different lengths (from real
cut-timing, not uniform) all push at the same visual pace instead of some
looking rushed and others barely moving. Capped at `MAX_ZOOM = 1.5` so an
unusually long segment can't push in far enough to look distorted. Segments
are rendered independently, concatenated via ffmpeg's concat demuxer, then
muxed against the mastered template audio — no MoviePy involved anywhere in
this pipeline, deliberately: the whole thing is pure ffmpeg CLI calls through
`core._run_ffmpeg`, since that primitive was already proven artifact-free in
the comparison tests and MoviePy's time-varying resize wasn't tested. Only
pip dependency is `requests` (via `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py`'s own
unconditional imports) — no librosa, no moviepy, no numpy, unlike every
other pipeline in this repo.

**Smoke-tested locally before relying on the real GitHub Actions run**: a
throwaway script (not committed) ran the full build chain — audio mastering,
cut-timing extraction, 14 push-in segments, concat, mux — against a local
stand-in video (`Inspiration video.mp4`, not a real Drive template) instead
of the real Meta/Buffer/Drive-credentialed path, to catch bugs before
spending a real live post on them. Produced a valid `11.91s, 1072x1920,
codec=h264` file, confirmed via `core.validate_reel_for_meta`; frames pulled
from four different points in the output confirmed clean hard cuts between
four different application photos with straight architectural lines
throughout (kitchen, mountain-lux kitchen, wabi-sabi bath, French powder
room) — the push-in reads correctly across a real multi-segment sequence,
not just a single isolated clip. **This stand-in video is a fast-cut source
(~0.7–1.0s segments, target zoom only ~1.05–1.07)** — noticeably faster than
the ~1.2s average segment length the main pipeline's own d-series reel run
showed (16 concepts in 19.8s, documented above). If a REAL Drive template
turns out to be similarly fast-cut, the push-in may read as barely
perceptible per segment; this is a pacing risk worth checking against the
actual first live run's real output, not something the smoke test could
rule out using a non-project stand-in video.

### Status and next step

`.github/workflows/dolly-reel.yml` — `workflow_dispatch` ONLY, deliberately
no `schedule:` trigger yet, same as every other brand-new content type in
this repo before it's trusted (`generate-concept.yml` follows the identical
pattern). **Per Dev's explicit instruction: the first manually-dispatched
run IS meant to be a real live post for his review** — not held back behind
a preview/approval step first. Once he approves that real run's actual
output (real post IDs on Instagram/Facebook/TikTok/YouTube, and the push-in
pacing judged against the real segment lengths a real Drive template
produces), a `schedule:` trigger gets added here, same promotion path every
other pipeline in this repo has already gone through.

### The first real dispatch failed, and it exposed a repo-wide bug, not a Dolly Reel bug

The first `workflow_dispatch` run (2026-08-18, 16:28 UTC) built a completely
valid reel — real Drive template (1/4), 31 segments from real cut-timing in
19.8s, every push-in clip rendered, concatenated, muxed, and validated
(`19.805167s, 1072x1920, codec=h264`) — then died one step later inside
`upload_video_to_public_host`'s own `git push`, with a plain non-fast-forward
rejection. **No post went out on any platform** — `publish_to_instagram` and
everything after it in `run_pipeline()` runs strictly after this push, so the
failure happened before any Meta/Buffer call was ever made, not mid-publish.

Root cause, confirmed from the actual commit timestamps, not guessed:
Carousel Post's own Tuesday/Friday 16:00 UTC schedule fired independently and
pushed "Add carousel images 1787070659" at 16:30:59 UTC, landing on `main`
while this Dolly Reel run's OWN local commit (made from a checkout taken
several minutes earlier) was still sitting unpushed, waiting on 31 segments
to render. When it finally tried to push at 16:32:12, origin had moved out
from under it. **This is a real, repo-wide bug that has nothing to do with
Dolly Reel specifically** — every one of the (now five) pipelines in this
repo commits and pushes straight to `main` with a bare `git push` and no
retry, and this project now has multiple independent schedules plus
workflow_dispatch, all capable of overlapping in the same few-minute window.
It was only a matter of time before two of them collided; Dolly Reel's
unusually long build time (31 individually-rendered ffmpeg segments) just
made the collision window wide enough to actually hit for the first time.

**The fix**: `core._git_push_with_retry()`, a shared helper that retries a
failed push with `git pull --rebase origin main` in between attempts (5
tries, short backoff) instead of dying on the first collision. All four
existing raw `git push` call sites in `core_decor_reel_pipeline.py`
(`_write_and_commit_counter`, `advance_caption_index`,
`upload_video_to_public_host`, `upload_images_to_public_host`) now route
through it. This protects every pipeline in the repo, not just Dolly Reel —
if a future pipeline adds its own raw `git push` instead of reusing this
helper or one of the four functions above, it will reintroduce exactly this
failure mode the next time two schedules overlap.

### The second and third dispatches both hung on `apt-get install ffmpeg` — switched to a static binary

After the git-push-retry fix landed, two more manual dispatches (16:36 and
16:44 UTC) both hung indefinitely on the workflow's `sudo apt-get update &&
sudo apt-get install -y ffmpeg` step specifically — everything before it
(checkout, Python setup) completed in seconds both times, then this one step
never finished, confirmed genuinely stuck rather than just slow by polling
past 9+ minutes with no change and confirming the in-progress job's logs
return `BlobNotFound` (not a step-status reporting lag — the step's own
`status` field stays `in_progress`, which flips immediately on real
completion regardless of when logs get archived). `githubstatus.com` showed
no active Actions incident at the time, so this reads as ordinary apt-mirror
flakiness on that specific package, not a GitHub-wide outage. Both stuck
runs were cancelled via the Actions API rather than left to time out on
their own.

**Fix**: replaced the apt install with `FedericoCarboni/setup-ffmpeg@v3`, a
marketplace action that downloads a static ffmpeg binary directly instead of
going through apt/the package mirror network path at all. Only changed in
`dolly-reel.yml` for now — `daily-reel.yml` and `hot-takes-reel.yml` still
use the apt-based install and it worked fine on both of their most recent
real runs today, so this wasn't touched as a blanket fix, just the workflow
that was actually failing. If apt-based ffmpeg installs start failing on
OTHER pipelines too, that's the signal to swap the rest of them over to the
same static-binary action rather than assuming this fix alone covers it.

### First successful live run — 2026-08-18, confirmed on all four platforms

The next dispatch after the ffmpeg fix went end-to-end clean: real Drive
template 1/4, 31 segments from real cut-timing in 19.8s (application images
1-31/57), every push-in clip rendered, concatenated, muxed, validated, and
published:

- **Instagram**: media_id `18057315959790065`.
- **Facebook Reels**: video_id `1441858494772822`, post_id
  `122122986159091378` — verified delivered length 19.8s matches expected
  (`_verify_facebook_video_duration`), confirming the concatenated-segments
  approach doesn't trip the historical Facebook truncation bug (see that
  section above) now that publishing goes through the Reels pull-based API.
- **TikTok via Buffer**: post_id `6a848eb9af0852fb78ea185f`.
- **YouTube via Buffer**: post_id `6a848ec46723dcd0cf4892a0`.
- All three counters (`application_index.txt` 0→31, `template_index.txt`
  0→1, `caption_index.txt` 0→1) committed and pushed cleanly on the FIRST
  attempt, no collision this time — `_git_push_with_retry()` exists for when
  one happens again, not because every run hits it.

**Awaiting Dev's review of the actual posted video** before adding a
`schedule:` trigger to `dolly-reel.yml` — per his explicit instruction, this
live run itself was the test, not a preview step.

### Real bug found from watching the actual posted video: zoom drifted top-left to bottom-right instead of centering

Dev's own review of the live post caught it immediately: every clip read as
sliding from the top-left toward the bottom-right rather than pushing
straight into the center. Root cause: `_pushin_clip()`'s `zoompan` filter
call never set `x`/`y` — ffmpeg's zoompan defaults BOTH to `0`, which
anchors the shrinking crop window at the source's top-left corner. As zoom
increases, that corner stays pinned in place while everything else grows and
gets pushed outward and off-frame — exactly the "drifting toward
bottom-right" look, repeated identically on all 31 clips since every one
used the same unset default.

**Fix**: added the standard centered-zoom expressions,
`x='iw/2-(iw/zoom/2)':y='ih/2-(ih/zoom/2)'`, which keep the crop window
centered on the source at every zoom level. Verified locally before
re-running live: rendered a 3s test clip on the same `c01_kit_modlux_app.png`
image, pulled the first and last frame, confirmed the pendant light/
countertop/window all grow proportionally in place around the same center
of composition instead of sliding toward one corner.

**Worth remembering for any future ffmpeg `zoompan` use in this repo**: the
filter's `x`/`y` default to `0`, not centered — every call needs those two
expressions set explicitly, or it silently reproduces this exact bug. This
wasn't caught by any of the earlier comparison tests (`test_a_kenburns.mp4`,
the smoke test) because nobody was specifically looking for directional
drift at the low zoom levels (~1.04-1.07x) those segments used — it only
became obvious to a human watching the real posted video with real playback
motion, not from inspecting individual static frames.

**Re-run after the fix, confirmed corrected**: same-day follow-up dispatch,
drew template 2/4 this time (only 9 segments across 19.9s — much slower
pacing than the first run's 31, so each push-in gets ~2.2s instead of
~0.6s, a real stress test for whether centering holds at a MORE noticeable
zoom level too, not just the fast-cut case). Published clean on all four
platforms: Instagram media_id `17952450183248438`, Facebook Reels post_id
`122122987113091378`, TikTok post_id `6a849331f43c887d411d5ba0`, YouTube
post_id `6a84933c8ec8f62532e920a2`. Counters advanced cleanly again,
`application_index.txt` 31→40, `template_index.txt` 1→2,
`caption_index.txt` 1→2.

**Second, unrelated infra flake hit mid-way through re-running this fix**:
the very next dispatch attempt (before the one that succeeded) hung on
`actions/checkout@v4` itself — not our own code, not even the ffmpeg step —
for several minutes before being cancelled. No GitHub-wide incident at the
time either. Between this and the earlier `apt-get install ffmpeg` hang,
that's three separate stuck-runner incidents in about an hour, on three
different steps, all resolved by cancel-and-redispatch rather than any code
change (except the one genuine ffmpeg-to-static-binary fix). Worth knowing
if a future dispatch just sits at "in_progress" with no step progressing
for several minutes: check `githubstatus.com` first, but don't assume it's
this repo's code without checking which step is actually stuck — a
transient runner issue and a real bug look identical from run status alone
and need the per-step timestamps to tell apart.

### PROMOTED TO PRODUCTION — 2026-08-18

Dev's verdict on the corrected re-run: "Its great push it live." `dolly-
reel.yml` now has a real `schedule:` trigger (`0 10 * * 1,4` — Monday and
Thursday, 10:00 UTC), same promotion path every other pipeline in this repo
went through: build it, dispatch it manually, fix what a real live run
exposes, get an explicit approval, then and only then make it scheduled.
Placeholder day/time, same status as every other schedule in this repo —
revisit once there's engagement data. `workflow_dispatch` stays available
alongside it for manual test runs going forward.

This is now a FULLY LIVE, five-pipeline repo: the original swatch+
application daily reel, Hot Takes, Single Product Reel, Carousel Post, and
Dolly Reel — each with its own schedule, own counters, own state, publishing
independently to Instagram/Facebook plus TikTok/YouTube/Pinterest via
Buffer where wired.

## Shop the Look — a monetization page, not a content pipeline (2026-08-18)

Dev's actual monetization state going in: an Amazon Associates Linktree with
**zero revenue so far**. Root cause diagnosed in conversation, not guessed —
the posted content (generic AI room concepts) and the affiliate links (real
Amazon products) were completely disconnected; nothing a viewer just watched
was actually clickable/purchasable. Dev also flagged that featuring real
products in NEW renders costs real BFL generation money, ruling out "just
regenerate everything with real products in frame" as the quick fix.

**What this is**: `shop/` — a static page, not a pipeline, requiring zero
new AI generation. Reuses the EXISTING 57 application photos already live in
reels/carousels (referenced directly from `assets/application/` via
raw.githubusercontent.com, the same zero-cost hosting pattern used
everywhere else in this repo) and lets Dev attach real affiliate links to
each one after the fact. A viewer who recognizes a room from a video now has
somewhere real to click.

**Files**:
- `shop/products.js` — one entry per concept (`id`, `image`, `room`,
  `style`, `productName`, `productUrl`), generated programmatically from the
  actual `assets/application/` filenames (room/style codes decoded via the
  same naming convention documented above under "Concept asset naming"), not
  hand-transcribed. **`productName`/`productUrl` are deliberately `null` for
  all 57 entries** — real affiliate URLs were never fabricated or guessed;
  only Dev can fill these in with his actual Amazon/affiliate links.
- `shop/shop.js` — renders only products WITH a `productUrl` set; a card
  with `productUrl: null` is skipped entirely, never shown broken. Appends
  `utm_source=coredecor&utm_medium=shop_page&utm_content={id}` to every link
  on click, so which concepts actually convert is trackable without Dev
  manually tagging each link himself. `rel="sponsored"` on every CTA link
  plus a footer disclosure line — Google/FTC affiliate-link requirements,
  not optional styling.
- `shop/style.css` — matches the swatch-card brand register (dark editorial,
  Fry's Baskerville for headings via the SAME font file already hosted at
  `concept_tools/fonts/FrysBaskerville.ttf`, no new asset).
- `shop/README.md` — how to add a real product (edit one entry in
  `products.js`, push — no build step, no deploy step).

**Hosting**: GitHub Pages was already enabled on this repo (root of `main`,
serving `data-deletion.html`/`privacy-policy.html` for Meta app compliance)
— confirmed via the Pages API before assuming it needed setup, not guessed.
`shop/index.html` is now live at
`https://devdave666.github.io/core-decor-automation/shop/` with no
additional configuration.

**Verified locally before pushing**: served the page with `python -m
http.server`, screenshotted with headless Edge (`msedge.exe --headless
--screenshot`, no browser automation framework installed — this environment
has Edge at
`C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe`, no
Chromium/Playwright). Confirmed the zero-links empty state reads cleanly
(not broken/blank), then temporarily patched one entry with a fake test
product+URL to confirm card rendering (image, room tag, style title, product
name, tracked CTA button) before reverting `products.js` back to the clean
all-`null` state via a backup diff check.

**Still needed before this earns anything**: Dev has to actually go through
his Amazon Associates account (or a higher-commission network — see the
earlier monetization discussion in this session about Amazon's 1-4% home
goods rate vs. 8-20% via LTK/ShareASale/Awin for DTC home brands) and fill
in real `productName`/`productUrl` pairs. This page is the mechanism, not
the revenue — it earns nothing until real links are added.

### `shop/admin.html` — in-browser editing, added same day after Dev asked for it directly

Dev asked for a way to click a blank card and fill in the product directly,
rather than hand-editing a file. Two things had to change to make that safe:

- **`products.js` → `products.json`.** A `.js` file with comments (the
  original ships had inline `// e.g. "..."` guidance comments) can't be
  safely read-modify-written by a script without risking corrupting the
  formatting or silently dropping the comments. Pure JSON round-trips
  losslessly. `shop.js` was updated to `fetch("products.json")` instead of
  relying on a `<script src="products.js">` global — confirmed this still
  works via a fresh headless-browser screenshot before moving on, not
  assumed from the code alone.
- **`shop/admin.html` + `admin.js` + `admin.css`** — a separate page, not
  linked from the public `index.html`, so casual visitors never see it.
  Gated behind a GitHub fine-grained personal access token the user creates
  and pastes in themselves: stored ONLY in that browser's `localStorage`
  under `coredecor_shop_admin_token`, sent only to `api.github.com`, never
  written to any file or committed anywhere. The token is scoped to
  **Contents: Read and write on this one repository only** — the page's own
  first-run screen walks through creating exactly that token, not a
  broader classic PAT, deliberately narrower than the automation token
  already in `env.template` (principle of least privilege — this token
  living in a browser's local storage is a meaningfully different risk
  profile than one living in a GitHub Actions secret).
- Save flow always re-fetches the file's current `sha` immediately before
  writing (via the GitHub Contents API), rather than reusing whatever `sha`
  was loaded when the page first opened — avoids clobbering a change made
  from another tab or device in between.

**A real bug was caught before shipping, not after**: the modal and the
toolbar both rendered VISIBLE despite `hidden` being correctly set on them
via JS. Root cause, confirmed via an actual headless-browser screenshot
showing the bug, not just reasoned about: `.modal-backdrop { display: flex
}` and `.toolbar { display: flex }` have the exact same CSS specificity as
the browser's built-in `[hidden] { display: none }` rule, and being defined
later in the author stylesheet, won the tie. Fixed with a single global
`[hidden] { display: none !important; }` rule at the top of `admin.css`.
**Any future admin-page style that sets its own `display` on an element that
can also be `hidden` needs this same rule in place, or it will silently
break again** — this isn't specific to the modal/toolbar, it's a property of
the CSS cascade that applies to any such element.

**Verified with a full mocked end-to-end test before trusting it**, not just
visual inspection: a throwaway local test harness (not committed) overrode
`window.fetch` to return canned data shaped like a real GitHub Contents API
response, pre-set a fake token in `localStorage`, then loaded the real
`admin.js` unmodified. Screenshotted three states: the grid rendering
correctly with a mix of linked/blank cards, a card click opening the modal
correctly pre-filled with that concept's existing data, and — the real test
— programmatically filling the modal and clicking Save, confirming the
status line updated to "Saved c02 — live in about a minute," the card
re-rendered with the new data and a LINKED badge, and the modal closed, all
with no thrown JS errors. This is the same rigor already established
elsewhere in this project (Dolly Reel's smoke test, the carousel image-prep
checks) — a UI that LOOKS right in one screenshot isn't the same as one that
actually completes its core interaction.

## Amazon Creators API — real credentials tested live, confirmed blocked (2026-08-18)

Dev asked for a fully automatic pipeline: search each application photo on
Amazon, find similar products, auto-link them. Real constraints surfaced
before any of that got built (see the "quicker revenue"/"programmatically
search" conversation earlier the same day): Amazon has no image-similarity
search API at all — only keyword search — and the only programmatic path
(what turned out to be Amazon's new **Creators API**, not the classic
PA-API) has a real eligibility gate. This section is the record of actually
testing that gate against Dev's real account, not assuming it from docs
alone.

### What the Creators API actually is

**Replaces PA-API 5.0 outright — PA-API is being retired May 15, 2026**
(Offers V1 inside PA-API goes first, January 31, 2026; Offers V2 only
exists in the Creators API). Confirmed from Amazon's own docs
(`affiliate-program.amazon.com/creatorsapi/docs`), not a third-party
summary alone. Genuinely different from PA-API in three ways:
- **OAuth2 client_credentials grant** instead of AWS Signature V4 — a
  `client_id`/`client_secret` pair gets exchanged for a 1-hour Bearer token
  at `https://api.amazon.com/auth/o2/token`, scope `creatorsapi::default`.
- **New host and path shape**: `https://creatorsapi.amazon/catalog/v1/
  searchItems` (confirmed by hitting it directly — `creatorsapi.amazon.com`
  doesn't even resolve, and the old `webservices.amazon.com` host returns a
  generic Amazon error page, not a Creators API response).
- **lowerCamelCase fields** (`itemIds` not `ItemIds`), unlike PA-API's
  PascalCase.
- **Eligibility**: confirmed from Amazon's own docs — **10 qualifying
  Associates sales in the past 30 days**, stricter than PA-API's old
  3-sales/180-days rule mentioned earlier in this session before the actual
  Creators API migration was discovered. This is the number that matters
  now; the earlier 3/180 figure is obsolete.

### Dev supplied real credentials mid-conversation — handled per this repo's existing credential discipline

Dev uploaded `Core_Decorcredentials.csv` (columns: `Application`,
`Application Id`, `Credential Id`, `Secret`, `Version` — a real OAuth app
registration, `Application: Core_Decor`, `Version: 3.1`). Two things done
before touching it: confirmed `env.template` is `.gitignore`d (`git
check-ignore -v env.template` — real check, not assumed) before writing
anything to it, and never printed the raw secret or the resulting access
token anywhere in a chat response — every test script masked both to a
few characters on each end.

**Tested live against Amazon's real servers, not just read about**:
1. Token request succeeded — real Bearer token issued, `expires_in: 3600`.
2. A real `SearchItems` call against the confirmed-correct endpoint
   returned `{"reason":"AssociateNotEligible","type":"AccessDeniedException"}`
   — proof the credentials, endpoint, and request shape are ALL correct,
   and the only blocker is Amazon's own sales threshold. This matters:
   without testing live, "not eligible" and "wrong endpoint/malformed
   request" look identical from the outside, and only one of those is
   fixable by writing better code.

**Credentials stored as encrypted GitHub Actions secrets**
(`AMAZON_CREATORS_APPLICATION_ID`, `AMAZON_CREATORS_CREDENTIAL_ID`,
`AMAZON_CREATORS_SECRET`) using the same libsodium sealed-box encryption
GitHub's API requires (`PyNaCl`, fetched the repo's public key via
`GET .../actions/secrets/public-key` first) — the same mechanism GitHub's
own UI uses, not a workaround. `AMAZON_ASSOCIATE_TAG` (`dev0f7d-20`, the
Associates "-20" tracking tag Dev provided) was stored as a plain
repository **variable**, not a secret — deliberately, since it's not
sensitive on its own (it's embedded in every public affiliate link already)
and using the Variables API rather than Secrets API for it is the correct
distinction, not laziness. `env.template` got the same three credential
names added but left BLANK, matching every other credential in that file
except `GITHUB_TOKEN` — the file's own stated philosophy is values "only
ever pasted into a chat transiently and never stored by me," and there was
no reason to break that pattern just because the values happened to be
available in this session. `AMAZON_ASSOCIATE_TAG` alone was filled in with
its real value locally, since it isn't a secret.

### What got built, ready but dormant

- `shop/amazon_creators.py` — reusable `get_access_token()` /
  `search_items()`, raising `AmazonCreatorsError` with a `.reason` field so
  callers can distinguish `AssociateNotEligible` (expected, not a bug) from
  a genuine failure.
- `shop/check_eligibility.py` — run any time to check whether the account
  has crossed the threshold yet. Exits 0 on "not eligible yet" (that's the
  expected steady state, not a failure) and only exits non-zero on a real,
  unexpected API error.
- `.github/workflows/check-amazon-eligibility.yml` — `workflow_dispatch`
  only, runs the above without needing a chat session at all.
- **Verified functionally before considering it done**, not just
  `py_compile`-checked: ran the actual production script locally with the
  real credentials loaded into ephemeral subprocess env vars (never written
  to any file, never printed) and confirmed it correctly reports "Not
  eligible yet" with exit code 0.

**Deliberately NOT built yet**: the actual "search each concept's photo,
propose matching products" pipeline Dev originally asked for. Building that
against an API that will reject every single call right now would be
wasted effort with no way to verify it actually works end-to-end — the
right time to build it is once `check-amazon-eligibility.yml` reports
success for real. Until then, the realistic path to filling in `shop/
products.json` is the manual SiteStripe + admin-tool workflow already
built, which has the added benefit of being what generates the qualifying
sales that unlock this in the first place.

## Search-keyword hints + tightened manual workflow (2026-08-18)

With the Creators API confirmed blocked, Dev asked to make the manual
SiteStripe workflow itself as few clicks as possible — "give me an amazon
link, click on it, go to amazon, copy affiliate link and paste that back
somewhere, making it 2-3 click operation."

**`shop/products.json` gained a `searchKeywords` field on all 57
entries** — a concrete, specific description of the real object actually
visible in that concept's photo (e.g. "wagon wheel wrought iron candle
chandelier" for c36, "oxblood burgundy velvet wingback armchair" for d01),
generated by looking at every one of the 57 application photos directly,
not guessed from the room/style name. Several of these were spot-checked
against real Amazon inventory via live web search before trusting the
vocabulary (confirmed real listings exist for "cloud bubble glass cluster
pendant light", "fluted brass cabinet pulls art deco", "wagon wheel
wrought iron candle chandelier", "pleated fabric drum pendant light",
"oxblood burgundy velvet wingback armchair", "black arc floor lamp black
marble base" — all returned multiple real, current Amazon listings, not
zero-result searches).

**The admin page's modal now drives the actual workflow**, not just data
entry:
1. Opening a blank card pre-fills the product-name field with a
   title-cased version of the suggested search term (still editable) and
   shows the raw search term above the buttons.
2. **"1. Search on Amazon"** — `window.open`s Amazon's own search results
   for that exact term in a new tab. Disabled if a concept has no
   `searchKeywords` (shouldn't happen now that all 57 have one, but the
   fallback is there for any future concept added without one).
3. SiteStripe → Text → Copy happens on Amazon's page — this step is
   genuinely NOT automatable from here; it's the only way to generate a
   real affiliate-tagged link without Creators API access, and it lives
   entirely inside Amazon's own UI.
4. **"2. Paste link from clipboard"** — reads `navigator.clipboard.
   readText()` (a real Clipboard API call, not a fallback) and fills the
   URL field automatically. Validates the pasted text loosely (contains
   `amazon.` or `amzn.to`) and shows a warning rather than silently
   accepting a wrong paste, but still fills the field either way — trusts
   the human's judgment over blocking on a regex.
5. A `visibilitychange` listener arms itself the moment "Search on Amazon"
   is clicked, and adds a pulsing glow to the paste button the instant the
   tab regains focus — so coming back from Amazon makes the next action
   obvious without having to remember the flow. One-shot: removes itself
   after firing, and again on modal close, so it doesn't leak listeners
   across cards.

Five clicks on this page's side (card → Search on Amazon → \[SiteStripe on
Amazon, out of our control\] → Paste from clipboard → Save) is the real
floor without programmatic search — verified against what's actually
possible, not a made-up target.

**Verified with a full mocked end-to-end test, same rigor as the first
admin build**: a throwaway harness (not committed) mocked `window.fetch`
(GitHub Contents API), `window.open` (records calls instead of navigating),
and `navigator.clipboard` (returns a realistic SiteStripe-shaped URL) via
`Object.defineProperty` — bypasses real browser clipboard permissions
entirely rather than fighting headless Chromium's permission model, and
loads the real, unmodified `admin.js`. Drove the full sequence
programmatically and dumped the DOM at the end via
`msedge.exe --headless --dump-dom`: confirmed the name field prefilled
correctly, the suggested-search box showed the right text, `window.open`
was called with the correctly URL-encoded Amazon search, the paste button
picked up the `pulse` class after a simulated `visibilitychange`, the
clipboard mock's URL landed in the URL field with a "Pasted." notice, and
Save completed with the status line and modal both updating correctly —
every step of the real interaction, not just a static screenshot.

## Fix: shop admin was generating amazon.com links, not amazon.ca (2026-08-19)

Dev reported "Shop This Look" style links kept redirecting to amazon.com.
Root cause: Dev's Associates account is approved for **Amazon.ca only** (not
yet qualified for the US program — same 10-sales/30-day threshold that
blocks the Creators API, see above), but `admin.js`'s "Search on Amazon"
button opened `www.amazon.com/s?k=...`, so any SiteStripe link copied from
that search carried a tag that wouldn't earn commission under this account.
`amazon_creators.py`'s `search_items()` had the same wrong default
(`marketplace="www.amazon.com"`), which would have repeated the bug once
Creators API access unblocks.

Fixed both to `.ca`. Also tightened `admin.js`'s paste-clipboard check: it
now distinguishes "not an Amazon link at all" from "an Amazon link but the
wrong marketplace" (`amazon.com`, `amazon.co.uk`, etc.) and shows a specific
warning for the latter, rather than treating any `amazon.*` domain as fine.
`products.json` had no real links saved yet (all `productUrl: null`), so
nothing existing needed correcting — this was caught before any bad link
went live.

**Smart location-based redirect** (route a US visitor to amazon.com, a UK
visitor to amazon.co.uk, etc.) was also asked about. Answer given: that's
Amazon's own **OneLink** feature (Associates Central), not something to
build as custom geo-IP logic — but OneLink only pays out through
marketplaces where Dev actually holds an Associates tag, and right now
that's `.ca` alone. Revisit OneLink once the US Associates program clears,
not before. See `shop/README.md`'s new "Amazon.ca vs Amazon.com" section.

## Interactive shop hotspots: click-a-dot-on-the-photo, multiple items per room (2026-08-19)

Dev asked two things in one message: (1) why the shop admin only ever
surfaced the light fixture per photo, not other furniture/decor in frame,
and (2) build a car-dealership-style interactive hotspot UI — translucent
dots on the application photo, click one to jump straight to that item's
Amazon listing. Also: Dev's US Amazon Associates account is now active
alongside the existing Canada one.

Asked Dev two scoping questions before building (via AskUserQuestion, not
guessed): who identifies the extra shoppable items in the 57 existing
photos (chose: Claude drafts them first, via image analysis, for Dev to
review/reposition/link), and how the admin should pick US vs CA per link
now that both accounts are live (chose: per-item toggle, default US).

**Schema change**: `shop/products.json` — each concept's single top-level
`productName`/`productUrl`/`searchKeywords` became a `hotspots` array.
Each hotspot has its own `id`, `x`/`y` (percentage position on the photo),
`label`, `productName`, `productUrl`, `marketplace` (`"us"`|`"ca"`), and
`searchKeywords`. A concept only shows on the public page if at least one
hotspot has a real `productUrl`; only linked hotspots render a dot.

**Coordinate math decision that mattered**: the photos are ~1072x1920
(portrait), but the site's cards used `aspect-ratio: 4/5; object-fit:
cover`, which crops ~15% off the top and bottom. Storing x/y against the
raw image and rendering with that crop would have desynced every dot from
where it visually sits. Fixed by dropping the crop entirely — both
`shop/style.css`'s `.card img` and the admin editor's image now render at
native aspect ratio (`width:100%; height:auto`, no `object-fit`). This
means a hotspot's x/y percentage is the same number in the admin editor and
on the live site, no conversion needed. Don't reintroduce `object-fit:
cover` on either without redoing this math for all 227 existing hotspots.

**Public page** (`shop/shop.js`): each linked hotspot renders as a pulsing
translucent dot (`.hotspot-dot`) positioned absolutely on the photo, with a
hover tooltip showing the item name and a direct link (target `_blank`,
`rel="noopener sponsored"`) to its tracked Amazon URL. A plain-text link
list underneath each photo duplicates the same links as a non-hover
fallback (mobile, accessibility, crawlability) — dots alone aren't
guaranteed discoverable. UTM tracking now uses `{conceptId}-{hotspotId}`
as `utm_content` so per-item click-through is measurable, not just
per-photo.

**Admin page** (`shop/admin.js`, `shop/admin.html`, `shop/admin.css`):
clicking a grid card (now badged `linked/total` instead of a binary
LINKED/blank) opens a full-photo editor. Existing hotspots show as dots —
solid for linked, dashed for pending. Click a dashed dot to open the edit
modal (same SiteStripe search-and-paste flow as before, now with a
**US/CA marketplace toggle** that changes which `amazon.<tld>` domain the
"Search on Amazon" button opens and what the paste-clipboard mismatch
check expects). Click empty photo space to create a brand-new hotspot at
that point. **Drag any dot to reposition** — implemented with Pointer
Events (not native HTML5 drag-and-drop) so it works the same for mouse and
touch; commits the new x/y via the same GitHub Contents API PUT the rest of
the admin already uses, save-on-drop with no separate confirm step.
"Delete hotspot" removes a dot entirely (for AI-drafted items not worth
pursuing); clearing just the URL field and saving unlinks without deleting
the dot.

**227 hotspots drafted for the 57 existing photos** by a background
general-purpose agent (not by directly reading all 57 images inline —
would have blown up this session's context): read each photo, kept the
existing light-fixture `searchKeywords` verbatim as hotspot #1, identified
2-4 additional prominent purchasable items (rugs, chairs, faucets,
mirrors, cabinet hardware, vases, etc.) with plausible Amazon search
phrasing and an estimated x/y position. Validated programmatically before
merging: all 57 ids present, every array 2-5 items, all coordinates in
[0,100], no missing label/searchKeywords. The agent flagged 8 concepts
(c05, c12, c21, c26, c33, d01, d02, d04) where the *original* light-fixture
`searchKeywords` actually described a different object entirely (a data
quirk from however those were first authored, e.g. c05's "light fixture"
keywords were really a kitchen faucet) — relabeled to match what the text
actually describes rather than silently leaving a wrong label. These are
a first draft, not verified pixel-by-pixel against the photos — expect
Dev to reposition/relink/delete some while going through them.

**amazon_creators.py**: default `marketplace` param flipped back to
`www.amazon.com` (was briefly `www.amazon.ca` from the single-account fix
earlier this session) now that both accounts are live and US is the
chosen default — still unused/blocked by the Creators API eligibility gate
either way.

**Verified before calling this done**, not just written and assumed
working: `node --check` on both JS files; a headless Edge
(`--headless=new --dump-dom`) render of the public page with one hotspot
temporarily linked confirmed the dot's `style="left:52%;top:22%"` and
tracked `href` matched exactly what was set, then the fixture was
reverted; a from-scratch mocked-fetch test harness (same technique as the
original admin.js test — `window.fetch`/`navigator.clipboard` mocked, real
unmodified `admin.js` loaded) drove the full click-empty-space →
fill-fields → Save → reopen → Delete sequence end-to-end against a fake
GitHub Contents API and asserted on the resulting JSON (20/20 checks
passed) before the harness file was deleted; a final headless render of
both real pages (all-real, all-unlinked `products.json`) confirmed the
empty-state message on the public page and a clean token-gate load on
admin with no console errors.

Still not done: OneLink (Amazon's native geo-redirect across marketplaces)
isn't wired up — noted in `shop/README.md` as the right next step once
there's real traffic, not built speculatively now.

## Hotspot accuracy fix + snap-to-grid tool (2026-08-19, same day as the hotspot feature)

Dev came back after using the admin page live (see the "Shop admin: reposition"
/"update"/"delete" commits he made directly through the deployed old and new
admin.js while this session was in progress -- merged in cleanly, see below)
and said the AI-drafted hotspot positions were mostly wrong: "misplaced almost
all marks." His fix suggestion: a visible grid overlay in the editor, dots
placed at grid intersections, and "tighter" grid than whatever default I'd
reach for. He'd already hand-corrected `c03` through the admin UI and named
it as the accuracy bar to match, and asked for `c01`-`c05` as a test batch
before approving a pass over the rest.

**Diagnosis before fixing anything**: rendered the *actual saved* hotspot
coordinates as crosshairs directly onto each photo (PIL, temp `_check_*.png`
files, viewed and deleted after) rather than trusting written x/y numbers or
re-deriving positions from prose descriptions -- that's what actually showed
where a dot lands vs. guessing from percentages. Most of c01/c02's dots were
already close; the real misses were c04's kitchen faucet dot (landed on the
window frame, not the faucet -- moved ~2-3% right/down) and c05's "Cabinet
Pulls" hotspot, which was flat-out mislabeled: it sat on a small stone/mineral
bookend decor piece, and this photo's minimalist brutalist cabinets don't
have visible pulls at all. Relabeled to "Stone Bookend Decor" with matching
search keywords rather than leaving a hotspot pointing at nothing real.

Fixed c01/c02/c04/c05 (16 hotspots total) by looking directly at each photo
and hand-placing pixel-accurate positions, snapped to a clean grid, then
re-rendered the crosshair overlay again to confirm before considering it
done -- same verify-by-rendering approach as the diagnosis step, not just
"edited the JSON and assumed it's right."

**New admin feature** (`shop/admin.html`, `shop/admin.css`, `shop/admin.js`):
the hotspot editor now shows a faint reference grid over the photo (CSS
`repeating-linear-gradient`, cell size driven by a `--cell` custom property)
plus a **Grid tightness** range slider (10-80 cells, default 40 = 2.5% cells,
remembered in localStorage per-browser). Both click-to-create and
drag-to-reposition now snap to the nearest grid intersection (`snap()` in
admin.js, rounds to the nearest cell) instead of landing at the raw cursor
position -- this is the actual fix for "misplaced marks" going forward, not
just a one-time data correction. Verified with a from-scratch mocked-fetch
test harness (same pattern as the original admin.js tests): default grid
renders at the right cell size, the slider changes it live, a click snaps a
new hotspot to the expected grid intersection, and a drag snaps an existing
one at a different (tighter) grid setting -- 9/9 checks passed before the
harness file was deleted.

**Remote sync note**: while this session was paused (user hit a usage limit
mid-task) and again between turns, Dev kept using the live admin page --
merged in three separate rounds of his real edits (`git fetch` + `git merge`,
never `--force` or `-X ours`) rather than overwriting them: 4 real product
links for c01-c04 added through the *old* pre-hotspot admin.js (folded into
`hotspots[0]` for those concepts, `marketplace: "ca"`), then his own manual
c01-c04 repositioning and c03 additions/deletions through the *new*
hotspot-editor admin.js once it went live. Always `git fetch` and check
`git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main` before pushing on this repo now --
Dev actively edits `products.json` through the deployed admin page in
real time, independent of whatever's happening in a chat session.

c06 through c50 and d01-d07 still carry the original AI-drafted positions,
not yet reviewed at this new accuracy bar -- waiting on Dev's approval of
c01-c05 before doing the rest.

## Hotspot positioning finished for all 57 concepts + auto-generated affiliate links (2026-08-20)

Continuation of the previous entry's accuracy fix. Dev kept fixing concepts
himself live through the admin page throughout this work (c01-c20 and
d04-d07, 24 concepts total, including adding a brand-new 5th hotspot to d04
that was still unlabeled/unlinked when this entry was written) -- his edits
were always treated as authoritative and fetched/merged before every push,
never overwritten. The remaining 33 concepts (c21-c50, d01-d07) were
verified and corrected using the same render-crosshair-and-look loop,
split across three rounds of background agents (52 -> 33 -> 7 concepts as
scope narrowed) plus 7 done directly in this session when the last batch
of agents ran out of runway. Every one of the 233 hotspots across all 57
concepts is now verified against its actual photo, not estimated from a
text description alone.

**Lesson learned about background agents on this task, worth remembering
before delegating similar long-running work again**: three separate rounds
of agents got killed mid-run by session-limit resets and one container
restart, and the first round lost 100% of its work (two full 17-concept
batches) because they were instructed to write output only once at the
very end. Fixed by requiring incremental saves (read-merge-write the output
file every 2 concepts) in the next rounds -- when those also got cut off,
partial progress survived and only a handful of concepts needed redoing
instead of the whole batch. Also: agent IDs from a killed/restarted session
are NOT resumable via SendMessage ("No transcript found") -- don't bother
retrying resume, just relaunch fresh with narrower scope covering only
what's confirmed missing on disk.

**Reverse-engineered real affiliate links from Dev's own examples**: Dev
provided one real SiteStripe-generated link for each marketplace --
confirmed the tag for `.com` is `dev0f7d00-20` and for `.ca` is
`dev0f7d-20` (two different tags, one per Associates account -- distinct
from the tag mentioned in the earlier "Amazon Creators API" section of
this file, which was a placeholder/example value, not this real one). His
US example was actually malformed for this purpose (a bare
`amazon.com?&linkCode=...` homepage link with no `/s?k=` search path,
apparently generated via SiteStripe's generic "Get Link" without searching
first) -- didn't copy that mistake; built proper `/s?k=<terms>` search
links using his `.ca` example as the correct template for both
marketplaces.

Wrote a link-generator (`build_url()` in a one-off script, mirrored as
`generateSearchLink()` in `shop/admin.js`) that builds
`https://www.amazon.<tld>/s?k=<terms>&linkCode=ll2&tag=<real tag>&linkId=
<random 32-hex>&ref_=as_li_ss_tl` (plus `&language=en_US` for `.com`,
matching Dev's example). Backfilled all 228 hotspots that had
`searchKeywords` but no `productUrl` yet -- the shop page went from a
single linked concept (4 hotspots) to all 57 concepts live with 232/233
hotspots linked in one pass. Confirmed via a real headless-browser render
that the page shows all 57 cards, 232 dots, and correctly-tagged/tracked
`href`s before pushing.

These generated links are real and commission-tagged but point to search
results, not one exact ASIN -- a deliberately lower bar than a hand-picked
SiteStripe link. Marked with `"auto": true` on the hotspot (228 backfilled
ones have it; Dev's 4 originally hand-linked ones don't) so the distinction
isn't lost. Wired the same generator into the admin modal itself as an
explicit **"Generate a tagged search link instead"** button (deliberately
NOT an automatic fallback on every save -- that would have broken the
existing "clear the URL field to unlink" behavior, since almost every
hotspot has `searchKeywords` filled in). The editor's marker styling now
has three states: solid = real curated link, dotted = auto-generated
search link (`.is-auto`), dashed = unlinked (`.is-pending`) -- the dotted
state is the visual todo-list for "find the real product and upgrade this
one." The `auto` flag is tracked/cleared automatically based on which
button last touched the URL field (paste vs. generate vs. manual edit),
verified with a 12-check mocked test (real per-marketplace tag/host
switching, flag set on generate, flag cleared on paste-over).

One bug caught during that test-writing, not by inspection: `admin.js`'s
first draft of `generateSearchLink()` used `encodeURIComponent()` for the
search terms, which encodes spaces as `%20` -- inconsistent with the
Python backfill script (`urllib.parse.quote_plus`, which uses `+`, matching
Dev's own real link examples). Fixed to build the query string via
`URLSearchParams` instead, which encodes spaces as `+` like the rest of
the project. A second test failure (paste-clipboard silently not updating
the URL field) turned out to be `navigator.clipboard = {...}` not actually
overriding the read-only property in headless Chromium -- needs
`Object.defineProperty(navigator, "clipboard", {value: ..., configurable:
true})`, not a plain assignment, to mock it (the earlier admin.js test
harness in this file's history already knew this; re-learned it the hard
way here since a new harness was started from scratch instead of copying
the old one forward).

## Compressed shop images for a snappier page + Instagram bio readiness check (2026-08-20)

Dev asked if the shop page was ready to link in his Instagram bio. Checked
for real rather than assuming: fetched the actual live production URL
(not localhost) and confirmed it serves the current `products.json` (57
concepts, 232/233 hotspots linked), then checked mobile rendering.

**Worth recording since it wasted real effort**: the first mobile check
(headless Edge `--window-size=390,3200 --screenshot`) showed the header
title and the per-item pill list clipped at the right edge, looking like a
real horizontal-overflow bug. It wasn't — confirmed via an iframe-based
diagnostic (load the real page in a 390px-wide iframe, walk every element's
`getBoundingClientRect()`, check for anything exceeding the viewport) that
`document.body.scrollWidth` was 390, exactly matching the viewport, with
zero real overflow. The only element geometrically exceeding the viewport
was an invisible `.hotspot-label` tooltip (`opacity: 0`, only shown on
hover) -- harmless. A follow-up screenshot of that same iframe rendered
perfectly. Conclusion: headless Edge/Chrome's direct top-level navigation
under `--headless=new` applies some viewport-meta-driven zoom/shrink
heuristic that a plain `--window-size` doesn't fully suppress, and it was
never actually representative of real mobile rendering. Trust the
DOM-measurement diagnostic (iframe + scrollWidth/getBoundingClientRect)
over a direct headless screenshot for mobile-viewport checks on this
project going forward -- don't repeat the false alarm.

**Image compression**: the 57 application photos are ~3.4MB PNGs each
(190MB total) -- fine for the reel/carousel pipelines they were made for,
heavy for a mobile shop page even with `loading="lazy"`. Confirmed via
`grep` that `assets/application/*.png` is a real dependency of
`carousel_pipeline.py` and the `daily-reel`/`carousel-post` GitHub Actions
workflows before touching anything -- so the originals were left
completely untouched. Instead, re-encoded all 57 to WebP quality 85
(Pillow, `method=6`) into a new `assets/application_web/` directory:
190MB -> 17.3MB, a 90.9% reduction, visually confirmed near-lossless on a
sample (details like marble veining and pendant-light glass texture held
up fine). `shop/products.json`'s `image` field for all 57 concepts now
points at the `.webp` copies instead of the `.png` originals via
raw.githubusercontent.com. `assets/application/` itself and every other
pipeline reference to it are unchanged.

Also asked about a free custom domain for the bio link, since the current
URL is the unbranded `devdave666.github.io/core-decor-automation/shop/`.
Answered honestly rather than oversell it: GitHub Pages *hosting* is free
regardless, but actually *owning* a custom domain name always costs
something from a real registrar (~$10-15/year, sometimes promotional
first-year pricing) -- there's no legitimate way around that; free
domain-giveaway services (Freenom etc.) were deliberately not recommended,
they have a bad reputation for reclaiming domains and being used for abuse.
Real zero-cost alternatives offered: a URL-shortener with a custom alias
(e.g. Bitly), or restructuring to a GitHub User Page
(`devdave666.github.io` at the root instead of the current
`/core-decor-automation/shop/` project-page path) for a shorter
still-github.io link -- both free, neither is a real custom domain.

## Hot Takes: daily schedule + opinion pool 44 -> 94 (2026-08-20)

Dev reported Hot Takes performing really well and asked to increase
frequency and add more dialogues, explicitly wanting it "very interesting
and scroll-stopping" — same "follow the real numbers" logic already
recorded above for why Hot Takes exists at all and why d09's palette was
trusted.

`.github/workflows/hot-takes-reel.yml`: cron `"0 18 */2 * *"` (every 2
days) -> `"0 18 * * *"` (daily), same 18:00 UTC slot so it still doesn't
collide with the main daily-reel's 14:00 UTC run. Checked the other
workflows' schedules before changing this (`daily-reel.yml` 14:00 UTC
daily, `dolly-reel.yml` Mon/Thu 10:00 UTC, `carousel-post.yml` Tue/Fri
16:00 UTC) — daily brings Hot Takes to parity with the flagship format,
not past it; going to 2x/day wasn't done here since there's no engagement
data yet justifying that big a jump, and it would burn the opinion/caption
pools twice as fast for no confirmed benefit. Worth revisiting once there
are real numbers at the new cadence.

`hot_takes/opinion_bank.py`: `OPINIONS` 44 -> 94 (+50), matching the
2026-08-18 expansion's exact constraints (documented above and in the
module's own docstring) — every new entry still passes the DELIBERATELY
GENERIC test (no color/material references, checked programmatically with
a regex sweep for the obvious offenders — beige/brass/marble/black/white/
gold/walnut/oak/velvet/linen/wood/concrete/leather — as well as by eye),
still a two-line setup/punchline pair (load-bearing for the 1.6s reveal
gap in `render_text_block`), still a mix of "They: dismissive / Me:
pushback" and standalone philosophical-statement pairs rather than one
repeated joke shape. Sized the expansion specifically around the schedule
change: doubling posting frequency without growing the pool would have
meant every opinion repeating twice as often, undoing a lot of the
"feels fresh" benefit the frequency increase was meant to capture.
Verified before committing: `len(OPINIONS)` == 94, zero exact-duplicate
pairs, zero malformed (non-2-tuple or empty-string) entries, YAML itself
parsed and re-checked for the correct cron string and that
`workflow_dispatch` survived the edit (it's a sibling of `schedule:` under
`on:`, not nested inside it — easy indentation mistake to introduce here).

## Facebook "reach" investigation: root cause was follower count, not publishing method (2026-08-20/21)

Dev suspected Meta was throttling reach on API-published Facebook posts
specifically, based on a hunch after enabling Instagram's "auto-share to
Facebook" setting. Investigated with real API calls against real
production data rather than guessing or trusting docs alone (Meta's own
Page/video Insights metrics are in active flux -- a batch was deprecated
June 15 2026 with limited warning, so doc summaries found via search were
treated as a starting point to verify against the live API, not as
ground truth).

**Step 1 — tested the actual premise**: confirmed via Meta's official
Content Publishing docs (fetched directly, not from memory) that the
Graph API's `/media`/`/media_publish` endpoints have no documented
relationship to Instagram's native "Share to Facebook" toggle at all --
that feature is part of the Instagram app's own publish flow, not exposed
to or triggered by the Graph API. A real test (published to Instagram
only via `SKIP_FACEBOOK_API`, see the workflow entry above) confirmed
this empirically: the post never appeared on Facebook. So "does the
native cross-post work for API content" has a clean answer: no, it
doesn't exist as a path at all, regardless of the toggle.

**Step 2 — checked whether API-published Reels get throttled reach
specifically, using real numbers**: pulled 7 real Facebook video_ids from
the last 6 days of production `daily-reel.yml` runs (extracted from
Actions run logs via `gh run view --log`, not guessed) plus the day's two
test posts, and queried `/{video_id}/video_insights` for each. Every
single one returned `{"data": []}` -- no error, just empty, uniformly,
including a video from 6 days earlier that had a full week to accumulate
views. That uniformity (not varying by post age or content) was the tell
